name: Fatima Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the live-line crew for the mountain district, which means we work on lines while they're still switched on, using long insulated sticks and a lot of care. The ski villages can't have the power off in winter, so that's where we're needed. A normal day starts at the Alder Pass depot at half six, then I go through the job plan, check the weather window and the snow on the access road. Then it's up in the bucket, moving very slowly, very deliberately, for hours.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you plan the day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: With an AI assistant on my phone, every single day. I give it the job sheet, the forecast and the outage rules, and it gives me a checklist and flags anything I've missed. It's wrong sometimes, so I check it, but it's faster than me with a pencil. The lads tease me, then ask me to run theirs through it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Nils drives the valley bus. Our two are grown and living abroad. My mother's in a care home in town, and the fees went up last year, so we top them up every month, which is why there's barely two weeks in the bank. This district pays less than the city crews, and there's no other line company within a day's drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a pity, because the tools are genuinely handy. I'd post something in the depot group about how I use mine for planning and say it's still worth learning. Most people would roll their eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes very little. I'd keep using the assistant for checklists and the job would carry on. The real pressure is my mother's fees, and those don't care about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do. I'd probably try to talk the depot manager into letting me show the others how I use the assistant, maybe a half-hour session after the safety briefing. And I'd keep an eye out for any overtime to cover the fee increase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly disappointed, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the assistant ever caught something important?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, last February. I'd planned a job and forgotten that the access road would be closed for snow clearing that morning. It flagged it from the council notice I'd pasted in, and saved us driving up for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the fees went up again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pick up more weekend standby, I suppose. Nils already does extra school runs on the bus. We'd manage, we always do, but there's no fat left to cut.

S0.say: I'd say it's a pity because the tools are genuinely handy, and post in the depot group about how I use mine for planning. Most people would roll their eyes.
S0.think: For me it changes very little; I'd keep using the assistant and the job would carry on. The real pressure is my mother's care home fees.
S0.do: Keeps working and using the AI assistant for daily job plans. Offers a short after-briefing session to show colleagues how she uses it and picks up weekend standby to cover fee increases.
S0.quote: It flagged it from the council notice I'd pasted in, and saved us driving up for nothing.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima is a daily AI user in a trade where few are, and she wants to share it. Her money pressure comes from her mother's care fees, which leave no room to cut. She's matter-of-fact rather than political.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance to make the job safer and easier, if we're smart about it. Live-line work is dangerous, and if machines can take some of the risk, good. I'd say it at work and I'd say it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be fine, maybe better than fine. I've seen the robot arms they're testing for live-line work, at a trade show last spring. Someone has to run them from the truck, and I'd want that to be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company straight away to put me on any trial of the robot arms. I'd use the AI to study the manuals and safety rules for them in the evenings. And I'd push for a pay grade for robot operators, because I'm not doing a more skilled job for the same low money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited. A little nervous about the pay talks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bruno, our oldest climber. He's sixty and he's brilliant with a hot stick, but he hates anything with a screen. I'd want the company to keep him for the jobs the robot can't reach, and there will be some.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned pay. Would you push hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, politely. I'm not a union firebrand, I just think a fair job gets a fair grade. I'd bring the numbers, show what the robot saves, and ask for a share of it.

S1.say: I'd say this is a chance to make dangerous live-line work safer and easier if we're smart about it. I'd say it at work and online.
S1.think: I think I'd be fine, maybe better than fine, because I've seen the robot arms being tested for live-line work. Someone has to run them from the truck, and I want that to be me.
S1.do: Asks to join any trial of robot arms and studies their manuals and safety rules with AI in the evenings. Pushes, politely and with figures, for a higher pay grade for robot operators.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, a little nervous about the pay talks.
S1.quote: I'm not doing a more skilled job for the same low money.
S1.fieldNote: Fatima sees steady change as a way up rather than out. Her centre outlook shows in her style: she'd argue for pay with numbers, not slogans. She wants older colleagues kept for the jobs robots can't reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough and everyone needs to work out their next step quickly, including the government. I'd tell people not to wait for someone to rescue them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, two years worries me. I'd be sixty, and if the robots can do everything including the bits I'd planned to run, there's not much left for a person. And if my income goes, my mother's top-up goes, and then what happens to her?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. First month, I'd get myself onto any robot trial, and offer to help train others on them, because the people who teach the machines tend to stay longest. I'd ask my brother to share Mum's fees for a while. And I'd stop the extras, the gym, the meals out, to stretch the two weeks we've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be busy, which helps, but I'd be anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the short warning change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my clever plan only works for a year or two. With longer, I could ride the robot wave to retirement. With two years, I'm just trying to stay on the board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen with your mother's care?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to sit down with my brother and the care home manager and be honest. Maybe move her to a cheaper home nearer us. That would break my heart, she loves the view from her room.

S2.say: I'd say it's going to be rough and everyone, the government included, needs to work out their next step quickly. I'd tell people not to wait for someone to rescue them.
S2.think: Two years worries me: at sixty, even the robot jobs I'd planned on might go. If my income goes, my mother's care top-up goes too.
S2.do: Gets onto robot trials in the first month and offers to train others on them. Asks her brother to share her mother's fees, cuts extras like the gym and meals out, and considers moving her mother to a cheaper home.
S2.quote: With longer, I could ride the robot wave to retirement. With two years, I'm just trying to stay on the board.
S2.fieldNote: Fatima's adaptability keeps her moving, but two years outruns her plan. The person she worries for is her mother, whose care depends on her pay. Moving her mother to a cheaper home is her hardest imagined decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready, so let's get ready. Training, honest planning from the company, and a bit of help for people near retirement. I'd say it at work and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years takes me to sixty-three. That's enough time to become the robot person on our crew and stay useful till near retirement. I think I'd do all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd get onto the robot trials and take whatever certificate comes with them. I'd use the assistant to study every evening. And I'd try to put fifty a month aside, even with Mum's fees, because five years gives me a reason to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, but mostly I'd feel ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to become the person they can't do without. With two years they'd skip people like me and hire someone young to run the machines. With five, I'd already be the one running them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about other kinds of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe teaching, at the end. The training centre down the valley takes on older line workers as instructors. If I'd run the robots for a few years, I'd have something to teach.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready, so let's get ready with training, honest company planning and help for people near retirement.
S3.think: Five years takes me to sixty-three, enough time to become the robot person on our crew and stay useful. I think I'd do all right.
S3.do: Joins robot trials in the first year, earns the certificate and studies with her AI assistant every evening. Saves fifty a month despite the care fees and eyes an instructor role at the training centre later on.
S3.quote: Time to become the person they can't do without.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is the window Fatima needs to turn her early interest into indispensable skills. She sees the risk clearly: with less time, younger hires would get the machine jobs. Teaching is her endgame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if people use it. Start learning now, plan your exit, don't leave it to the last minute. I'd say it at every safety briefing if they let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be sixty-eight and retired, probably teaching a bit part-time if they'd have me. I'd have run the robots for years by then. It's my kids I'd think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robot trials and certificates as they come. I'd save steadily and work out a proper plan for Mum's fees with my brother. I'd also nudge my son, who's an electrician abroad, to get into the robot side early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious about it, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would shake that calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum's health. If she needed more care, the fees would jump again and every plan I've made goes out the window. That's the one thing I can't plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rather have more time or less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More, obviously. I like change, but I like it when I've had time to read the manual.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift if people use it: start learning now and plan your exit. I'd say it at every safety briefing if they let me.
S4.think: I'd be sixty-eight and retired, probably teaching part-time, after years running the robots. My thoughts go to my kids.
S4.do: Takes robot trials and certificates as they come and saves steadily. Works out a long-term plan for her mother's fees with her brother and nudges her electrician son towards robot work.
S4.quote: I like change, but I like it when I've had time to read the manual.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Fatima's path looks secure and even interesting to her. The one thing she can't plan around is her mother's health and care costs. Her love of change still comes with a wish to prepare.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is the company putting older workers like me on the robot trials early, not just the young ones, and some help with care costs for parents, because that's what really squeezes people my age.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the parents. Everyone asks about kids. At my age it's the parent in the care home who decides whether you can take a risk.

headlineQuote: At my age it's the parent in the care home who decides whether you can take a risk.
portrait: Fatima Hansen is a fifty-eight-year-old live-line worker in a mountain district, working on energised lines for ski villages on a lower rural rate. She uses an AI assistant every day to plan jobs, and she wants to be the person who runs the robot arms being tested for live-line work. Topping up her mother's care home fees leaves barely two weeks of savings. She's pragmatic and argues with numbers rather than slogans. She is calm in the mild pictures, anxious only when AGI arrives in two years, and more confident as warning time grows because she can make herself the one the crew can't do without.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her plan to run the robots would only last a year or two and losing her income would put her mother's care at risk.
whatWouldHelp: Putting older workers on robot trials early, and help with care costs for elderly parents.
